Ben Thompson (@benthompson) on why we might run out of capital before we run out of demand for compute:

"I'm worried about the timing mismatch in terms of the actual return on investment producing enough revenue to fuel investment.

We're working our way down the capital curve. 

We started with free cash flow. The speed with which the tech companies blew through the debt markets is kind of incredible. 

It took like a year, and now Google's issuing equity. Nvidia's putting together this $500 billion thing to tap into pension funds and insurance floats and things like that. 

What's after that? Where does the money come after that?

Ideally we actually flip back to free cash flow funding this, but if there's a gap there, if we don't get there soon enough, then we could have a big blowup.

We don't have enough compute because there was insufficient investment made in 2023 and 2024.

So today, when you say there's not enough compute, all the money companies are putting in today doesn't equal compute tomorrow. It all goes into compute in 2029.

I believe in AI. I think it's a real thing. I think the economic impact is going to be astronomical.

You can believe all that and be worried about, are we going to make the bridge to this actually generating the level of returns necessary to continue to fuel this going forward?"

To better understand what happened today, we must first break down the price action.

At market open, stocks were down less than 1% and selling pressure began to build at 10 AM ET.

This was followed by a series of lower highs, which were followed by persistent selling pressure. https://t.co/pIsUm9nyQg

What just happened?

The Nasdaq 100 just posted its largest daily drop since the 2020 Pandemic, with the S&P 500 erasing -$3 trillion today.

Just 24 hours ago, the Dow surged +1,600 points after the Democrats "swept" the Midterms.

So, what changed? Let us explain.

(a thread) https://t.co/pf5ZW1Q9Qd

During days like today, investors need to ask: what fundamentally changed?

Why did the S&P 500 add +$1.2 trillion 24 hours ago then erase -$3 trillion today.

We dug into the potential fundamental drivers of today's decline.

One stuck out, but it still doesn't add up. https://t.co/La03PGN4Im

A post from a Democratic Congresswoman began as a mere opinion on X yesterday afternoon.

Today, this post has over 12 million views with several other members of Congress agreeing.

At the surface, markets could be pricing-in this supposed "ban," or strict regulation. https://t.co/DjnZ9ZTnZg

In our view, a ban of AI will not happen in the US (with near-certainty).

Such a ban, if even possible to enforce, would mean the US surrendering its position in the global AI race to China.

That won't happen.

We believe today's decline was more technical than fundamental. https://t.co/Ia0w0SJlOv

This is especially evident in how concentrated selling pressure was in chip stocks.

The S&P 500 excluding tech fell ~2.5% today while chip stocks fell nearly -11%.

The AI trade became "nervous" and today's downturn was a largely a product of fear and sentiment shifting. https://t.co/AO80HhYGpn

The market had already been concerned about AI profitability, CapEx, and Free Cash Flow.

After the election results, we saw a brief rally amid the $VIX crush.

However, as selling pressure mounted early today, sentiment shifted and these concerns were quickly exacerbated. https://t.co/Ig8wvQdsIv

The Volatility Index, $VIX, was further evidence of the emotional nature behind today's selloff.

Today's +63% rally in the $VIX marks the 5th largest spike in recent history.

We also believe several large institutional players were liquidated during today's trading session. https://t.co/7IfUjEnwvx

Then came the leverage.

Not only is leverage at a record, but investors bought the dip into Election Day with even more of it.

US levered ETFs attracted +$15 billion in inflows in October, their largest 1-month rolling inflow in at least 2 years.

This amplified today's drop. https://t.co/pbKobCOc7q

Lastly, technical corrections are healthy. 

Even a decline of 5-10% from current levels would be within a "healthy" correction.

History says Midterms are exceptional buying opportunities. 

The S&P 500 has returned +17.2% on average in the year following Midterms since 1950. https://t.co/9H4bG7IknH

This is why it is important to zoom out.

There will certainly be change in markets, the economy, and policy with the Midterm results.

However, this does not mean AI is "over." It is simply an adjustment.

We remain in the midst of the biggest technological revolution history. https://t.co/ma3UEHcxHA

A departure from my usual gloating:

If you lost all your money today, I'm sorry that happened. However you must understand that it was deserved. It means you had critical leaks in your trading and you need to take a break. Days like this happen infrequently but they will continue to happen for entirety of your trading career. 

Being levered is reserved for only the specialist of situations, you should almost never leverage. Never allow yourself to be in the position of a forced seller.

If you're having dark thoughts, or feel like you've taken 10 steps backwards and want to do something drastic, please don't. Life is far longer and opportunities are abundant.

Do not trade anytime soon. Go back and reflect on what your leak was (risk management, sloppy order placement, etc.) and learn. You paid your tuition.

If you continue trading without being self critical you are not a trader you are a PROBLEM GAMBLER.

Investing, trading and the journey to becoming wealthy rarely happens overnight. The only way to become profitable is to become your own harshest critic.

7 new things you should know about how ChatGPT searches for info (that will help your site optimization) ↓

1️⃣ ChatGPT now runs more fan-out searches per prompt, and the free and cheaper tiers are catching up to higher-tier models.

Fan-out means the AI autonomously rewrites your single question into multiple, hyper-specific sub-queries.

You ask: "What are the top gyms in Dubai?"
ChatGPT will search:

• Search 1: "top gyms Dubai 2026 reviews"
• Search 2: "Dubai gyms pricing comparison"
• Search 3: "site:https://t.co/H2MThwXEl9 best gym Dubai"

2️⃣ Being named in ChatGPT's first fan-out query drives a much higher chance of being cited: brands mentioned there were cited 68.9% of the time, versus just 2.1% for pages that were only fetched.

3️⃣ The number of unique domains cited per ChatGPT response dropped from 19 to 15 after the 5.3 update, even as more pages are retrieved.

4️⃣ Product pages now make up 16.39% of retrieved pages in ChatGPT fan-out queries, overtaking listicles.

5️⃣ For facts, ChatGPT fan-out queries go to official brand sites. For opinions and product reviews, they favor reddit and review platforms.

6️⃣ 21 of 27 ChatGPT initial queries contained brand names never mentioned by the user.

7️⃣ ChatGPT sometimes guesses the wrong brand domain, directing site: queries at parked or unowned domains, especially for lesser-known brands.

Practitioner notes based on the above:

1. Trying to create content to target individual fan-out queries is not a good strategy and can land you in Google's spam filters.

2. Monitor your site's impressions in search console tools to understand how often fan-out queries are reaching your site.

3. If your brand shares a name with other businesses or domains, consider adding 'Official Site' to your title or meta description to help ChatGPT and users identify the right site.

4. Make sure your key facts are in plain HTML on your brand's domain so ChatGPT can retrieve them via site: searches.

S/o to @lilyraynyc for this data; originally shared on Substack ↓
https://t.co/G0vRSFxibP

They kept the nuclear systems on this tech until like 2019. The FAA is phasing out now.

Super-secure slow-update tech like nuclear, air traffic, or banking, doesn't want to touch the outside world for as long as possible.

Given all this recent AI hacking news, you likely understand what I'm saying better than if I said it a year ago.

When existential systems are updated, it requires extreme vetting. Old tech is sometimes good, actually, if it's isolated and maintained as critical. https://t.co/nOt1Ni8gNH

Source: I worked for 12 years at the FAA in their simulation division for new technology.

The FAA isn't perfect, but much like the nuclear arsenal and major bank backups, you absolutely want to minimize overhauling the core system until you absolutely have to.

@HodlMagoo That's only partially true.

But it's also bureaucracy, funding, and risk mitigation. It takes decisiveness to change a system that's working.

The fact is tons of highly energized smart people were involved, but had to navigate around the existing context of a critical system.

@HodlMagoo It's similar to why nuclear generation sites don't have a ton of frequent updates.

Security over progress. Maintenance over innovation.

Not laziness, per se.

@SantiagoAuFund Exactly.

Bitcoin Core maintainers and hardware designers have to build with that intention in mind.

There's even a meme now that like people who bought 2010s-era hardware wallets and never updated are literally winning vs current hacks. Chad stuck with his tech.

Same idea.

The HMRC is still trying to frame my bank for money laundering and tax evasion to save face after the J5 investigation failed to show that my bank actually helped anyone evade taxes or launder money.

HMRC issued a press release about two men jailed for tax fraud. The fraud reportedly ran from 2016 to 2023, and HMRC says the men laundered money through 118 bank accounts, credit cards, and cryptocurrency trading platforms. Yet Euro Pacific Bank was the only financial institution named in the release.

I searched all 6,615 entries in my records of accounts that were open when my bank was shut down in June 2022. I checked both men’s names and the names of both companies they used. I found no matching account.

If either man or either company ever had an account at my bank, I believe we likely closed it before the shutdown. We closed thousands of accounts over suspicious activity. HMRC hasn’t identified the account holders or disclosed the dates of the transfers, so I can’t verify which accounts it’s referring to.

My bank was never fined for anti-money-laundering violations, and no one at the bank was criminally charged with any such violation. By singling out my bank and mentioning its shutdown, HMRC was trying to imply that my bank facilitated those crimes and that regulators shut it down for that reason.

https://t.co/gnGLubvxmD

HydroGraph’s MD&A contains a line worth revisiting:

“larger purchase orders and a long-term supply agreement within calendar 2026.”

That is management’s stated expectation—and 2026 is running out.

The October update adds substance: several advanced customer projects have reached negotiations over pricing, volumes and supply terms.

With 80+ customers engaged in development programs, which sector delivers first?

My strongest named candidate is protective coatings through Sparc Technologies. Extended corrosion-test results are expected in November, with successful results intended to lead into a commercial supply agreement. That makes Sparc particularly interesting—but it remains a candidate, not a confirmed order.

Conductive plastics are another contender, with Hubron, Broadway and Modern Dispersions already qualified as compounding partners.

Then there’s the timing: the court hearing is scheduled for November 10. Approval would remove another uncertainty around the planned U.S. redomicile, although completion remains expected in early 2027.

$SNAP Earnings: Back To The Free Perpetual Option Price

Market Cap: ~$9B | Earnings Reaction: -13%

$SNAP is back to roughly $5.20, the same price at which I initially recommended it, further reinforcing my original thesis: this is essentially a free perpetual option on Evan Spiegel finally making the right decisions.

Yesterday’s earnings showed revenue growth of 14%, adjusted EBITDA up 110%, and improving profitability and cash flow. On the negative side, advertising growth remains weak at 4%, stock-based compensation is still too high, and Spiegel has yet to make the strategic changes I want to see.

With 977 million monthly active users, $SNAP trades at just $9 per monthly user. Even comparing daily active users, the valuation gap is enormous:

$SNAP: ~$18 per daily user
$RDDT: ~$151 per daily user
$META: ~$442 per daily user

If $SNAP were trading at a $30 billion valuation, I would avoid it all together. But at just $9 billion, with improving profitability and cash generation, it’s hard for me to see the stock going substantially lower from here.

Unlike many growth companies, $SNAP doesn’t need to invent a new business or find hundreds of millions of new users. It already has nearly a billion users. It simply needs to monetize them better, something $META has beautifully demonstrated can be achieved through AI.

Evan Spiegel also needs to have the same realization Mark Zuckerberg eventually had about the metaverse: spending billions on a project doesn’t necessarily mean it will become a profitable business. The difference is that Specs actually have compelling real-world applications, but $SNAP needs a partner to share the costs, risks and development.

I believe Spiegel knows this. The day he announces a serious partner that de-risks Specs, I wouldn’t be surprised to see $SNAP jump 20% or more in a single day. And that’s just one of several possible catalysts, alongside better advertising monetization, reduced stock-based compensation and improved capital allocation.

None of these changes seems like a particularly tall order. Until then, perhaps $5-$6 is exactly where the stock deserves to trade. We’re essentially waiting for something to change, and if it does, the upside could be substantial. If it doesn’t, I believe the low valuation and enormous user base provide a meaningful margin of safety.

I recommended taking some profits when the stock rose from $5 towards $7 without any news to justify the move. Now that we’re back near $5, I believe the entry point is attractive again.

My Action: I’m Buying the Dip.

We’re starting to see measurable improvements in $SNAP ’s financial performance, and I believe the market’s 12% punishment following earnings was too harsh.

Of course, nothing is guaranteed. Spiegel could continue making the same mistakes, and the stock could remain depressed for years, but it’s hard to justify valuing a company with more than 900 million monthly users at less than $9 billion.

That’s what I mean by a free perpetual option. Heads, I win big. Tails, I barely lose.

$STAA: The Turnaround Continues

Market Cap: ~$1.5B | Yesterday Earnings Reaction: +9% | Last Month: +30%

For those unfamiliar with $STAA, STAAR Surgical is the global leader in implantable lenses for vision correction, an alternative to LASIK that doesn’t require removing corneal tissue. The company has a relatively strong moat, built on proprietary Collamer technology, regulatory approvals, decades of clinical data and relationships with eye surgeons. When it comes to your eyes, you’re not going to put something inside them that hasn’t been tested in other people’s eyes for at least 5 to 10 years. Competitors have faced safety problems with implantable lenses in the past that where considered “the next big thing”, making STAAR’s long clinical track record a substantial competitive advantage.

I initially recommended $STAA at $17.50, following the proposed $30.75 acquisition by Alcon, which was opposed by Broadwood Partners, a hedge fund owning approximately 30% of the company, on the grounds that the offer was too opportunistic.

Yesterday’s earnings further reinforced my investment thesis. Revenue reached $83.4M, representing 21% underlying growth, with China up 31% and Europe up 31%. Adjusted EBITDA improved to $14.4M, net income reached $5.6M, and cash increased to $206M with zero debt. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached $270.5M and adjusted EBITDA $58.8M. Management also authorized a $50M share buyback.

Gross margins remain under pressure at 70.9%, but management expects improvement beginning in Q4 and continuing into 2027.

Once that is learned, everything changes, because it also teaches how to take the hits.

Getting banged up is fine, but getting knocked out of the game is not. The willingness to get banged but not knocked out of the game is a big part of that.

The NASDAQ has already given back all of its post-midterm gains, down another 3% today.

Similar thing happened in 2018.

Lot of exuberance following the midterms in 2018 (SPX rallied 2% the next day), then 3 major events caused the market to sell-off into December.

1) A Hawkish Fed: In October 2018, Fed Chairman Jerome Powell remarked that interest rates were still a long way from neutral, signaling to investors that the Fed would continue tightening monetary policy into 2019 regardless of cooling economic data. This triggered severe liquidity fears and widespread panic selling.

This is similar to today in that the market is pricing in 2 more rate hikes despite the sell-off we have seen in tech.

2) Escalating U.S.–China Trade War : Just before and after the midterms, a flood of major multinational companies (including Caterpillar, 3M, and Ford) warned that rising tariff costs were eating into their profit margins and disrupting global supply chains.

This is similar to today as tariffs have had major inflationary effects and is one of the reasons why the Fed has to remain hawkish.

3) Tech Valuation Reversals: The technology sector, which had been the primary engine driving the multi-year bull market, abruptly reversed course in late 2018. We also had the FAANG slump in which major tech giants faced severe regulatory scrutiny over antitrust and data privacy concerns (such as Facebook's controversies).

This is similar to today as the AI trade has taken quite the breather with AI fears mounting.

History does not always repeat itself, but it does often rhyme.

The market is treating a Dem sweep as an existential threat to AI infrastructure. It’s not.

Data centres can (and already are) being built outside the US. Hyperscalers have major footprints and active expansions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Canada and LatAm. Power, speed of permitting and cost drive site selection more than pure US policy.

If domestic buildouts slow, capital will simply reallocate. Global AI compute demand doesn’t disappear because Northern Virginia or Texas gets harder to permit. Latency-sensitive training prefers concentrated clusters, but inference, regional capacity and a large share of workloads work fine abroad.

The nutty part is the indiscriminate selling of the whole growth stock complex. High-quality, FCF-positive AI names and infrastructure software companies with multi-year visibility are getting lumped in with pure high-beta, negative-FCF builders that actually do have financing and execution risk. 

Policy friction in one country ≠ the end of the AI buildout.

International optionality is real.

There were about 10,000 new venture funds started between 2019 and 2022.

They have not done well.

That money went deep and wide. Little seed groups everywhere.

What happened? Markets shifted. Returns compressed. Competition exploded.

Most of those funds won't raise a second fund.

That's the reality of venture: It looks easier than it is.

From the outside, it's "just invest in startups." From the inside, it's judgment, timing, relationships, and conviction through the J-curve.

The funds that survive will be the ones that differentiate. That built real advantages.

Not the ones that just showed up with capital.

Market Thoughts 6 Nov 2026 - Equities Bloodbath

- At this point, it is quite clear that the trade is over, and has been over for quite some time; Today was the day people decided to *all* rush to the exits in no order whatsoever

- Retail momo was the first to go a few months ago, with Space stocks and Quantum all crashing. Then now is the time for semis. 80% of the S&P has been in a bear market the past few months; the 20% are now joining them.

- In general, the way I see it now is that it has all been one giant liquidity cycle; In a K-shaped world, money flows to the top 20% of assets that keep the game going, and in this case, it was all in AI; now that the music has stopped, money is flowing out and getting destroyed. 

- This comes after the fact that the Fed has started a new hiking cycle, you have rising costs of living, a war that hasn't stopped and is devastating for the real economy, and it's all now showing up in real time through a blue sweep in midterms

- But of course, the present is already priced in. Now all that's left is what's next. Sadly this sorts of demand destruction is incredibly hard to recover from - you need time. Now that everyone is poor again, you'll need time for some of these assets to bottom out

- I believe that there are certain sectors that are also still forming rounded tops - financials being one; so in general over the next few weeks / months we should be seeing more down moves. 

- Is the AI trade dead though? As assets bottom out, it would be obvious to start picking your horses for the eventual success of the buildout. I do think this is true, but it's going to take time to show who genuinely wins. As the cost of intelligence becomes cheaper and cheaper, it's pretty clear that the whole "infrastructure wins because volume explodes" also isn't as good of an explanation anymore as infrastructure gets better and better. Gun to my head, the winner of better intelligence would instead be the companies that learn to leverage this intelligence into real world outcomes instead (e.g Biotech)

- What's the next trade? It looks pretty grim now, for most sectors. At times like this, it's much better to let the market show its hand, but if you really want a decisive answer, going by the charts, digital assets still look the best - although this has been said for the 20th time; 

- Somehow, every week there is a new "maximally bearish" event and Bitcoin fails to break below 76k. Even if it does break, I have a feeling it's going to fake-out and reclaim. 

- But from a fundamental standpoint there seems to be no good reason for digital assets to do well. So far, most investors I've asked have backward looking indicators that would justify a pump in hindsight, but doesn't necessitate any sort of buying pressure now. Examples include: 4 year cycle lows, relative strength to equities, or cheap fundamentals 

- I will say that the most bullish case I can think of is that akin to software, digital assets are uniquely situated in how they can leverage AI to build more economical output much quicker. In a time where the market is starved of any sort of positive catalyst, digital assets are seeing breakneck rates of adoption e.g Druckenmillers investment into Trade[XYZ], tokenization of stocks, equity perps, ICE partnerships, etc. 

- It would be thus incredibly offside if investors didn't allocate 1-2% minimally into what is potentially a new emerging trend in the markets while everything else crashes. The world hates the previous iteration of crypto, but with this new adoption and people waking up to its usecases, price may follow

Overall though, the best thing to do now is probably remain mostly flat, with a small portion of one's book allocated to these new emerging trends. And the larger portion waits until the time is right to allocate into the death knell of some of these assets that will be 10x'es in half a decade.

The current $VVV chart is extremely reminiscent of the May-June distribution pattern, with sudden strong bursts getting completely retraced and printing lower highs (see yesterday's brutal pump-and-dump).

Last time, there was a perfect support/resistance level retest at $10 which gave an entry for a +250% move

The same scenario here could be a retest of $18 for example.

After such a wild multiple (up 30x bottom to top), I would normally be very bearish on the token but they are now buying back $50k+ worth of tokens daily and the size of the buybacks has been going up only, so yeah it makes sense for people to pick VVV as an alt long when they go want to go risk-on...

But for now, the chart remains bearish, and it's probably safer to keep this bias until there's something constructive showing up.

Why has today been so bad?

You had multiple sell side analysts on Wall Street come out this morning and basically say the same thing, which is that they are starting to believe capex growth will now peak in 2027. This doesn’t mean capex will stop, but the rate of growth for it will peak in 2027.

This means the rate of growth for semi earnings could be perceived as topping as well. 

At the same time, the market doesn’t know if the Fed will continue to be aggressive with their tightening.

Neocloud debt continues to yield higher, with CoreWeave now having yields at 17%. 

The result is a market sell off across the board. Nvidia is down 9%.

No one believes in the future earnings or low P/Es because if datacenters can’t come online, the revenue itself won’t be there to justify the capex.

The bright side is that mean hyperscalers pull back capex and FCF goes positive sooner than expected along with yields eventually coming down due to lack of new AI debt, but that means semis continue to sell off in that scenario. 

Worst day all year for the Nasdaq.

The new UX is the API. The new user is an agent. For decades, the best product builders were the ones who understood humans better than anyone else.

Building great software meant having a really good intuition for UX. Will people know where to click? Can they find the right action? Is the product intuitive?

A lot of the best builders developed that intuition as teenagers building websites, then spent years learning what makes software easy to use.

But now we're building for agents, and it's a completely different skill set. Take booking a business trip. For humans, you build a nice interface to search flights, pick a hotel, add things to your calendar and submit expenses.

For an agent, none of that matters. What matters is whether it can figure out which APIs to call, understand the parameters, handle errors, and complete the whole thing without getting stuck halfway through.

An API can make perfect sense to an engineer and still be terrible for an agent. So for example, imagine an API where creating a calendar event, inviting attendees, booking a meeting room and setting permissions are four separate operations. Perfectly logical from an engineering perspective. But now an agent has to discover the right sequence, understand dependencies, handle partial failures and clean up if something goes wrong. Why not let it express the entire intent in one call and have the system handle the rest?

I think we're going to see a new generation of product builders who have incredible intuition for how agents think, what confuses them, and how to make software that they can actually use.

It's a new kind of product empathy (let's call it agent empathy, haha!)
